headline: Research shows that marine biology has always been a form of "big science"
dek: A historical analysis argues that large-scale scientific collaboration didn't begin with genomics — ocean biology has practiced it for centuries, from Darwin-era natural history expeditions to the Census of Marine Life.
summary_md:
## What they found

Long before the Human Genome Project sparked debates about whether biology was becoming "big science," naturalists were already doing it — mapping life on Earth through massive collective expeditions. This paper argues that **marine biology is a uniquely clear example of big science with deep historical roots**, and that the Census of Marine Life (CoML) — the landmark international project that inventoried life in the world's oceans — is the modern heir to that tradition.

The author traces a through-line from Darwin-era natural history voyages to CoML, examining how collaboration in marine research evolved across dimensions like **team size, internationalization, technology, and public communication**. The conclusion: marine biology is best understood as a transformed form of natural history — not a break from it.

## How they studied it

This is a historical and conceptual analysis rather than an experiment. The author reviews the development of marine research over time, using the Census of Marine Life as a central case study. By examining **multiple facets of collaboration** — how researchers worked together, how technology changed fieldwork, how findings were communicated to the public, and how the enterprise was internationalized — the paper builds an argument about what kind of "big science" marine biology actually represents.

Crucially, the paper introduces the idea of **"collective ways of knowing"** as a framework for distinguishing between different types of large-scale biological collaboration, suggesting this lens can sharpen how historians and sociologists of science understand big biology more broadly.

## Caveats & limits

- This is a **conceptual and historical paper**, not an empirical study with quantitative data — its conclusions rest on historical interpretation and argument, which are open to scholarly debate.
- The abstract does not specify which primary sources, archives, or datasets were used to reconstruct the history of marine collaboration.
- The claim that marine biology has been **overlooked** in big-science studies is asserted but not itself empirically tested in the abstract.
- The framework of "collective ways of knowing" is proposed as a new lens, but its broader applicability beyond marine biology remains to be tested by other researchers.

## Why it matters

The debate over "big science" in biology tends to treat the Human Genome Project as a turning point — the moment biology got big, expensive, and collaborative. This paper pushes back on that narrative, showing that **ocean scientists were running globe-spanning, multi-institution, technology-heavy collaborations long before genomics existed**.

That reframing matters for how we fund, organize, and talk about large scientific endeavors. If collaboration in biology has a much longer and richer history than the genomics debate implies, then **the lessons learned from centuries of natural history fieldwork** — not just from particle physics or sequencing centers — deserve a seat at the table when we design the next generation of big science projects.

It also quietly celebrates an underdog: field biology, often seen as low-tech compared to genomics or particle physics, turns out to have been quietly pioneering the social machinery of big science all along.
talking_point: Turns out the Human Genome Project didn't invent "big science" in biology — ocean researchers were running massive international collaborations since the days of Darwin.

paper.title: From Darwin to the Census of Marine Life: Marine Biology as Big Science
